summary:
Rotating right by k moves the last `k mod n` seats to the front, keeping both blocks in order. Reversing the
whole array, then reversing each of the two blocks, does exactly that in place: O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

question.md:
Move every seat k places toward the end, wrapping around to the front. Return the new order.

- **k can be huge** (up to 10⁹) but rotating by n is a full turn, so only `k mod n` matters. `[9, 8]` with
  k = 3 is the same as k = 1: `[8, 9]`.
- **k = 0** (or a multiple of n) leaves the order unchanged.
- **Goal:** in place with O(1) extra space.

think.md:
Take `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]` with k = 3. Each seat moves 3 places right; the last 3 seats wrap to the front:
`[5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4]`. In other words, the array is two blocks, `A = [1, 2, 3, 4]` and `B = [5, 6, 7]`, and the
answer is `B` followed by `A`.

think.caption: A B → B A, each block keeping its own order.

think.md:
Swapping two blocks of different lengths in place sounds hard, but reversal does it neatly. Reverse the
whole array: `B` comes first and `A` second, but each is backwards. Reverse each block again and both read
forwards. Every reversal is a simple two-pointer swap loop with O(1) extra space.

approaches.title: Rotate one step, k times

idea.md: One step right means: save the last seat, shift everything one place right, put the saved seat at the front. Do it `k mod n` times.

build: Repeat k times: save `a[n − 1]`, shift `a[0 … n − 2]` right by one, put the saved value at index 0.

lines.text: Only `k mod n` steps matter; full turns change nothing.
One step: the last seat is saved, everything shifts right by one (back to front, so nothing is overwritten early), and the saved seat goes to the front.

complexity.md: **Time O(n · (k mod n))**, up to O(n²). **Space O(1).**

steps.text: Step 1: the last seat moves to the front; everything else shifts right (7 moves).
Step 2: the last seat moves to the front; everything else shifts right (7 moves).
Step 3: the last seat moves to the front; everything else shifts right (7 moves).

walk.title: Turn the carousel one step at a time, k times: the last seat moves to the front.

limits.md: Each seat is moved k times by one place instead of once by k places.

approaches.title: Copy into a second array

idea.md: Seat i goes to position `(i + k) mod n`. Write every seat directly there in a new array.

build: For each i: `out[(i + k) % n] = slots[i]`.

lines.text: A second array of the same size.
Each seat jumps straight to its final position.

notes.java: `i + k` can pass 2³¹ when k is near 10⁹, so add in `long` before taking `% n`.
notes.cpp: `i + k` can pass 2³¹ when k is near 10⁹, so add in `long long` before `% n`.
notes.c: `i + k` can pass 2³¹ when k is near 10⁹, so add in `long long` before `% n`.

walk.title: Copy each seat straight to its new position (i + k) mod n in a second array.

limits.md: Needs a whole second array; the problem asks for O(1) extra space.

idea.md: With `k %= n`: reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k elements, then reverse the remaining n − k. The array was A B with |B| = k; the first reversal gives B' A' (both backwards); the next two give B A.

lines.text: Rotating by n changes nothing, so reduce k first (also keeps it a valid index).
Reverse a range in place with two pointers moving towards each other.
Whole array, then the first k, then the rest. With k = 0 the second reversal is empty and the other two cancel out.

notes.cpp: The standard `reverse` does the two-pointer swapping for us.

complexity.md: **Time O(n):** every element is swapped about twice. **Space O(1).**

steps.text: k = 3: the last 3 seats should end up in front, both blocks keeping their order.
Reverse everything: the last block is now in front, but both blocks are backwards.
Reverse the first 3: that block reads forwards again.

walk.title: Three reversals: the whole array, then the first k, then the rest.

takeaways.md:
- Rotation = swapping two blocks: **A B → B A**. In place: reverse all, then reverse each block.
- Reduce shift amounts with `k mod n` first.
- Rotate left by k is the same trick with the blocks split at k from the front.
